lessons.title: Constructing a philosophical argument: premises, validity, and charity
lessons.explanation: An argument, in the philosophical sense, is a set of propositions in which some, the premises, are offered as support for another, the conclusion. It is not an assertion, a report, or an insult. Two distinct virtues must be kept apart. An argument is valid when it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false; validity concerns the form of the inference alone. It is sound when it is valid and all its premises are true. Arguments that are not deductively valid can still be good: an inductive argument makes its conclusion probable, and an abductive argument infers the best explanation among competitors. Much real philosophy arrives in prose with premises unstated, so the first task is standardisation: identify the conclusion, list the premises that are explicitly offered, and then supply the implicit premises the argument needs to work. Doing that charitably, which means choosing the strongest reasonable reading before evaluating, is a methodological commitment rather than a courtesy, because it is the only way to avoid defeating a claim nobody holds.
lessons.example: Take a passage: ‘Of course she will eventually accept our theory of the case. Every careful person has, and she is careful.’ Reconstruct it. Conclusion: she will accept the theory. Premise one: every careful person has accepted the theory. Premise two: she is careful. As it stands the argument is invalid, because accepting the theory at some point in the future is not entailed by having been careful up to now; the conclusion needs a bridge. The charitable reconstruction supplies the missing premise: careful people who have examined the theory accept it, and she has examined it. With that premise added, the argument becomes valid in form, and the burden shifts to whether premise one is true, which is an empirical claim easily tested and easily doubted. Notice what standardisation accomplished. It converted a jibe into a testable argument and located the dispute at a specific premise, rather than at the rhetoric. It also revealed a hidden assumption about timing, which is exactly the sort of gap that makes bad arguments look persuasive. Inclusion of an implicit premise whose truth is doubtful is itself a legitimate criticism, provided the arguer would accept it.
lessons.question: What does adding an implicit premise to make an argument valid show about the original argument?
lessons.answer: That the original prose left a gap, and the burden now falls on whether the necessary added premise is true
lessons.distractor: That the original argument was meaningless and its author was not really arguing at all
lessons.correction: Unstated premises do not make an argument meaningless; they make it incomplete. Reconstruction makes the argument evaluable and shifts the dispute to the truth of the enounced premise.

depth.definitions: A premise is a proposition offered as support; the conclusion is what is supported. Validity is the property of a form in which true premises cannot have a false conclusion. Soundness is validity plus true premises. A counterexample to validity is a case with the same form in which the premises are true and the conclusion false. An enthymeme is an argument with an unstated premise or conclusion. Standardisation is the activity of setting an argument out as a numbered list of premises and a conclusion, supplying what is needed for the stated inference. Charity, or the principle of interpretational charity, directs you to adopt the strongest interpretation consistent with the text. Deduction, induction, and abduction are the main types of inference; an abductive argument recommends a hypothesis as the best explanation. Begging the question is arguing from a premise the arguer is entitled to only by already accepting the conclusion.
depth.mechanism: Why does charity earn its keep as method? Because the target of criticism is the truth of a claim and the strength of an inference, not the elegance of someone’s prose. If you refute a weak paraphrase, you have refuted nothing and have reinforced a false sense of superiority, which is the straw-man failure. The steelman discipline instead asks: what is the most defensible position here, and does it survive? There are limits, and the limits are methodological. Over-charity is a genuine risk: if you repair an argument so thoroughly that it becomes a different argument, you are no longer evaluating what was claimed, and the repair can quietly smuggle in premises the author rejects. The rule of thumb is to add only premises the author would endorse and to mark them as supplied. Equally important is keeping kinds of criticism straight. Showing a premise false is a different criticism from showing the inference invalid, and confusing them is the most common error in student work. A third discipline is separating an argument from its rhetoric: a well-organised ad hominem is still not an argument for the conclusion, and a badly expressed but valid argument is still valid.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a valid but unsound argument with an inductive argument. Valid but unsound: premises, all ferrous metals sink and this metal sinks, conclusion, this metal is ferrous. The form is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, so we must first repair or reject the inference; supplied charitably with the premise that only ferrous metals sink, it becomes valid, and then we can see that this premise is false, since aluminium is not ferrous. Now take an inductive argument: ninety-nine of a hundred surveyed bridges in the region passed a stress test, so the next bridge will probably pass. This has no deductive validity at all, yet it is a reasonable argument whose strength depends on sample size, representativeness, and base rates. The contrast teaches that ‘valid’ and ‘good’ are not the same, and that evaluating an argument requires knowing which kind of inference is being made. Treating a statistical inference as if it must be deductively valid is a category error, and it is a common way to dismiss legitimate arguments.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error is to call an argument invalid when in fact a premise is false. Validity is about the inference, and an argument can be valid with a false premise; the criticism should be aimed correctly. A second error is to accuse any argument whose conclusion appears among its premises of begging the question. Begging the question is a diagnosable vice, but a defence may legitimately use premises the opponent also accepts, and circular arguments can be dialectically useful in some contexts, which is why the charge needs argument rather than slogan. A third error is to assume that formal validity requires the words if and then to appear; many valid arguments have no conditional in them, and many invalid ones use the conditional carelessly. A fourth error is over-charity, reconstructing the argument so generously that you defend a view the author never held, which makes the exercise pointless.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: standardise this passage and evaluate it. ‘We should not teach critical thinking, because students who think critically challenge teachers, and disruption in classrooms harms learning.’ Model response: conclusion, we should not teach critical thinking. The argument is an enthymeme: the needed premise is that challenging teachers is always classroom disruption and that this harm outweighs the benefits of critical thinking, both of which are questionable. With those supplied, the inference is valid and the dispute shifts to the premises, where the first is clearly too strong and a counterexample is available. Self-review rubric: (1) did you list premises and conclusion in order? (2) did you mark every supplied premise as supplied? (3) did you aim your criticism at the specific premise you think fails? For a serious objection, argue the other side of the pedagogy question, granting the classroom-disruption premise and testing whether the conclusion follows anyway.
depth.summary: Arguments are premises offered in support of a conclusion, and the two virtues to track are validity of inference and truth of premises, with inductive and abductive arguments evaluated on their own terms. Standardising in charity converts prose into testable claims and locates the real disagreement. Retain three habits of this lesson: identify the conclusion, supply only premises the author would accept, and keep the criticism of inference separate from the criticism of premises. The next lesson takes the same materials and turns them into tools of criticism, testing principles with counterexamples and reducing positions to absurdity.

lessons.title: Evaluating arguments: counterexamples, reductio, and the strongest objection
lessons.explanation: Once an argument is standardised, there are only a few honest ways to attack it. You may attack a premise as false. You may attack the inference as invalid, and the standard way to do that is a counterexample: a case with the same form whose premises are true and whose conclusion is false. You may also use reductio ad absurdum, which assumes the target claim and derives a consequence the target’s own defenders must reject, thereby showing the claim cannot be held. For arguments about principles, the method of cases is central: you test a general claim, such as that knowledge requires certainty, by producing a case that satisfies the claim’s conditions and yet violates the intuition it was meant to capture, and you then repair the claim rather than abandon it. Fallacies are named patterns of bad inference, and they are useful, but naming one is not an argument. The label does work only when you show that the specific inference has the bad pattern and that the pattern is indeed bad here, which is why the most common abuse in argument is the confident invocation of a fallacy name.
lessons.example: Test a universal principle with counterexamples and then with a reductio, using a claim from earlier in the level. Candidate principle: a belief counts as knowledge only if it is certain, that is, only if it could not have been false. A counterexample presses this: consider your belief that you had lunch today. You could be wrong in elaborate scenarios, so by the principle you do not know it, yet the claim that you know it seems defensible and certainly is treated as knowledge in ordinary life. The counterexample shows the principle is too strong. Now use a reductio on a stronger neighbour: suppose that only what is certain is knowledge. Then no empirical belief about the external world is knowledge, since the sceptical scenarios of lesson seventy-three cannot be ruled out with certainty. But the principle was offered to preserve knowledge, and it delivers the opposite. Because the consequence is one the principle’s own defenders reject, the reductio succeeds against that formulation. Note what the two methods share: both locate the fault in a claim by deriving something the claimant cannot accept, and both then invite a repair, such as weakening the principle to fallible justification.
lessons.question: What must a reductio show in order to succeed?
lessons.answer: That the target claim, together with premises its defenders accept, entails a consequence those defenders must reject
lessons.distractor: That the target claim leads to a consequence the critic personally finds unpleasant or surprising
lessons.correction: The derived consequence must be untenable by the defender’s own lights. If it is merely unwelcome to the critic, the argument shows a disagreement about values, not an inconsistency in the target.

depth.definitions: A counterexample is a case inconsistent with a general claim, used to refute universal principles. A reductio ad absurdum assumes a claim and derives a contradiction or an unacceptable consequence, thereby refuting the assumption. A fallacy is a pattern of reasoning that tends to be bad; formal fallacies violate a rule of valid inference, informal fallacies are defective in content or context rather than form. Begging the question assumes a premise available only by accepting the conclusion. A false dilemma presents two options as exhaustive when they are not. Equivocation trades on a shift in the meaning of a term. A defeater is a consideration that undermines a justification or a claim. Burden of proof is the obligation to support a claim, and shifting it improperly is itself a defect in argument. Expressive inconsistency is the charge that one’s practice contradicts one’s stated principle.
depth.mechanism: Why is naming a fallacy usually insufficient? Because fallacy names are diagnoses of inference forms, and a form that is defective in one setting can be acceptable in another. Appeal to authority is a paradigm case: it is only fallacious when the authority is unidentified, irrelevant, or the field is one where expertise is not credible; citing a relevant, identified expert is a perfectly good evidential move, and the strength of such an appeal varies with the field’s consensus. Similarly, the correlation-causation warning is a caution, not a refutation; correlations can be strong evidence for causes, and refusing to reason from correlation is itself unreasonable. The discipline is to state the defect precisely: which inference, which premise, which alternative explanation is unaddressed. The same care is needed with the straw man. To show a straw man, you must display the argument the opponent actually made or would make and show that your target was weaker; merely disliking the position is not a demonstration. Finally, the strongest objections are the ones you would least enjoy receiving. A useful test is to write the objection as the defender would write it, with their best premises, and to see whether your criticism still bites; if it does not, you have found a criticism of a weaker view and should return to the drawing board.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a genuine question-begging objection with a charge of circularity that fails, so the distinction can be seen in operation. Suppose an epistemologist argues that a belief is justified just when it coheres well with a comprehensive system. A critic objects that the criterion is circular, since the belief that the criterion is right must itself cohere with the system. If the epistemologist replies that the criterion is offered as the correct analysis of justification and its defence may legitimately be the very sort of coherence it analyses, this is a disputed move, and the faithful description is that the coherentist accepts a form of theoretical circularity on principle while the objector treats any circularity as vicious. Contrast this with the Moorean reply in the scepticism lesson, where the defender asserts ordinary knowledge against the sceptical argument. Here the criticism that the reply begs the question must specify which question and show that the premise does work only because the conclusion is presupposed; the diagnosis is available but it must be argued, and it is contested whether Moore is guilty. Both cases teach the same point: circularity charges are arguments with premises, not exclamations.
depth.mistake: The commonest abuse is the drive-by fallacy label: accusing someone of a straw man or a false dilemma without showing that the alternatives are non-exhaustive or that the target was misdescribed. A second error is treating a defect in an argument as a defect in the conclusion; an argument can be badly presented and its conclusion true, and the failure of one argument leaves the conclusion standing until refuted. A third error is to assume that every dialectically asymmetrical situation has a unique correct burden of proof, when burden is often negotiable and can shift with what is agreed. A fourth error is to confuse an insult with a criticism: ad hominem criticism of a person’s character is relevant only if it bears on the reliability of their testimony about this matter, and noting that is not the same as dismissing moral criticism of conduct as a fallacy, which is itself a misuse of the fallacy label.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: a manager argues, ‘everyone on the team agreed, so the plan must be sound.’ Write the strongest objection and the strongest reply, keeping names of fallacies out of the objection text itself. Model response: the strongest objection is that agreement establishes consensus, not correctness, and consensus can arise from shared bias, deference to seniority, or absence of dissent; the objection is not merely that the argument is fallacious but that the bridge from agreement to soundness is missing. The strongest reply is that in the special case where the group is diverse, informed, and incentivised to disagree, agreement is real evidence, so the original argument is at best an enthymeme with an unstated premise about the quality of the group. Self-review rubric: (1) did you state the missing inference rather than name a fallacy? (2) did you give the best reply you could? (3) did you separate the quality of the argument from the truth of the plan? For a serious objection, consider whether there are conditions under which the number of people holding a view is itself a reason to hold it, and how those conditions would be tested.
depth.summary: Evaluation of arguments reduces to a small set of disciplined moves: refute a premise, refute an inference with a counterexample, or refute a claim by reductio, always in a form the view’s own defenders must reject. Fallacy names are shorthand for diagnoses that must be supplied, and the strongest objection is the one that engages the strongest version of the target. This concludes the method of the level. You now have a single toolkit used across all ten lessons: separate the semantic from the metaphysical question, state the strongest version of a view, locate the premise that does the work, and test it with cases. Apply it to any philosophical text you meet next.

questions.prompt: A theorist says a system could implement all the functional roles of pain with no inner feeling whatever. What does this claim do to functionalism?
questions.answer: It presses the objection that functional analysis may capture the role of a mental state without capturing its felt character
questions.distractor: It refutes physicalism by showing that mental states are non-physical properties of a single substance
questions.correction: The claim targets functionalism about experience, and many non-reductive physicalists accept the objection while remaining physicalists. It does not by itself establish property dualism.

questions.prompt: Someone argues that because moral codes differ across cultures, moral claims are merely expressions of approval. Which conflation should a careful reader flag?
questions.answer: It runs together observed variation, which is Mackie’s argument from relativity, with non-cognitivism about the meaning of moral sentences
questions.distractor: It assumes that moral codes never differ, which is contradicted by the historical record
questions.correction: Argument from relativity supports an anti-realist conclusion but does not establish the semantic claim that moral sentences are not truth-apt. These are distinct theses on different axes.

questions.prompt: A person born in a state and never having affirmed anything is treated by one theory as bound by a general duty to support just institutions. What is the particularity problem for that theory?
questions.answer: Such a general duty would bind the person to any just institution, not specifically to the state that governs her
questions.distractor: Such a duty cannot be stated without logical contradiction about who counts as a citizen
questions.correction: The duty may be perfectly coherent; the objection is that it is impartial rather than particular, so it cannot explain a bond to this state rather than to a more just one elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A passage argues that since careful readers accept the theory and she is careful, she will accept it. A student wants to refute it. What should the student do first?
questions.answer: Supply the implicit premise the inference needs, mark it as supplied, and then test that premise and the form
questions.distractor: Declare the passage invalid because it reaches a future conclusion from present evidence about the past
questions.correction: The gap is real, but the disciplined response is to reconstruct charitably and then attack the necessary premise or the repaired form, which locates the actual disagreement.

questions.prompt: A critic says an opponent is guilty of the straw man fallacy but gives no argument. What is missing?
questions.answer: The criticism must display the argument the opponent actually makes and show that a weaker version was targeted
questions.distractor: The criticism must show that the opponent’s conclusion is false, since a straw man charge implies the conclusion fails
questions.correction: A straw man charge is a claim about the treatment of an argument, not about the truth of its conclusion. Naming the fallacy is not yet an argument; the misdescription must be shown.

questions.prompt: A laboratory reports a true result from an instrument that, unknown to everyone, happened to display the correct figure while malfunctioning. Compare this with the Smith disjunction case and state the best verdict and the reason.
questions.answer: Both are cases of an accidentally true belief whose warrant does not connect to the truth-maker, so knowledge is lacking in the same way
questions.distractor: The instrument case is knowledge because instruments are usually reliable, whereas the disjunction case is not because testimony is weaker
questions.correction: Reliability in general does not repair this token case; what matters is whether the actual grounds connect to the fact that makes the belief true. The structure of the two cases is the same.

questions.prompt: Explain why a coherentist need not claim that truth is coherence, using the isolation problem as your starting point.
questions.answer: Justification can be a matter of fit within a system while truth remains a correspondence relation, precisely so that the system must have adequate input
questions.distractor: Coherentism does equate truth with coherence, and the isolation objection therefore leaves it untouched
questions.correction: Equating truth with coherence is exactly what makes the isolation objection fatal. Most coherentists keep truth as correspondence and address the input requirement separately.

questions.prompt: A politician says that because we cannot know for certain that a rumour is false, we must act as though it were true. Using the lessons on scepticism and on argument evaluation, identify the defects.
questions.answer: It treats a bare possibility as decisive and slides from lacking certainty about something to accepting a different claim, which the closure argument does not license
questions.distractor: It is refuted because the rumour is about the past, and knowledge of the past always rests on testimony
questions.correction: The relevant flaw is the inflation of possibility into defeat and the unlicensed inference, not the subject matter. Testimony about the past is ordinary evidence.

questions.prompt: A hospital must decide whether an advance directive binds a patient whose memory and personality have changed almost completely. Which theory would say the directive binds because the patient is the same individual, and what is its cost?
questions.answer: Animalism, which preserves the individual’s continuity but must explain why it subsumes the present person’s autonomy under an earlier decision
questions.distractor: Psychological continuity theory, which preserves the individual’s continuity by counting the patient as the same person throughout
questions.correction: Psychological continuity is precisely the theory that may find the patient no longer the same person. Animalism preserves identity, at the cost of a hard question about present autonomy.

questions.prompt: An agent acts exactly as she wanted to, but a hidden device would have compelled the same act had she wavered. What do compatibilists take from this case, and what remains contested?
questions.answer: It suggests that alternative possibilities are not necessary for responsibility, though it is contested whether manipulation of the agent’s history defeats responsibility
questions.distractor: It shows determinism is false, since a possible intervention means the future was never fixed in advance
questions.correction: The device is real in the scenario, so determinism is not the issue. The case bears on the principle of alternative possibilities, and the manipulation argument is the open pressure point.

questions.prompt: A debater claims a machine cannot be conscious because its states are only functional. Reconstruct this as an argument and identify the premise a physicalist would deny.
questions.answer: The suppressed premise that whatever is functionally analysable lacks felt character, which the non-reductive physicalist and the functionalist both contest
questions.distractor: The suppressed premise that machines cannot exist, which is plainly false and so the argument fails immediately
questions.correction: Nobody involved denies that machines exist. The disputed bridge is the move from functional analysability to absence of experience.

questions.prompt: Two philosophers agree that torture for amusement is objectively wrong but disagree about whether this truth exists independently of all practical reasoning. Which distinction are they drawing, and which positions do they occupy?
questions.answer: The distinction between objectivity, secured by a procedure, and stance-independence, so one is a constructivist and the other a robust realist
questions.distractor: The distinction between cognitivism and non-cognitivism, so one thinks moral sentences are truth-apt and the other does not
questions.correction: Both accept truth-aptness, so cognitivism is shared. The split is metaphysical, over whether objectivity requires a stance-independent fact.

questions.prompt: Use the particularity problem to explain why a general duty to support just institutions cannot by itself justify a state punishing a citizen who has refused to obey a just law.
questions.answer: The duty may support compliance with just institutions wherever they are, but it does not single out this state’s claim on this citizen, which is what punishment presupposes
questions.distractor: The duty is incoherent, so it cannot support any punishment, just or unjust
questions.correction: The duty is coherent but impartial. What is missing is the particular bond, which is exactly what Simmons locates as the gap in natural duty theories.

questions.prompt: A speaker says an argument is unsound because it is invalid. What is wrong, and how would you repair the criticism?
questions.answer: Soundness requires validity plus true premises, so showing validly-with-false-premise is the right target; state which premise fails instead
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, since invalid arguments can never be sound and so the criticism is automatically sufficient
questions.correction: The verdict may be correct while the reason is wrong. Precision matters: identify whether the inference or a premise is the defect, and supply the counterexample or the false premise.

questions.prompt: A critic refutes a claim by deriving a consequence that she personally finds distasteful, even though its defenders would accept it. Using the reductio standard, evaluate the criticism.
questions.answer: The reductio fails as stated, because the derived consequence must be untenable by the defenders’ own commitments, not merely unwelcome to the critic
questions.distractor: The reductio succeeds, because showing that a claim has unattractive implications is sufficient to refute it
questions.correction: Disagreement about an implication is not inconsistency in the target. A working reductio must derive something the view’s own supporters must reject.

questions.prompt: A student is told to steelman an opponent before replying. Explain what this requires and why it is a method rather than mere politeness.
questions.answer: Reconstruct the strongest reasonable version using only premises the opponent accepts; otherwise the criticism refutes nothing that was claimed
questions.distractor: Agree with the opponent’s conclusion first, then raise any objection that comes to mind, so that no reply is ruled out
questions.correction: Charity targets the strongest form of the argument and keeps supplied premises to those the author would endorse. Conceding the conclusion is not the method.

questions.prompt: Integrate the level: how should a careful reader handle a dispute where one side attacks a premise and the other asserts that the position is simply false?
questions.answer: Standardise the argument, mark supplied premises, keep attacks on premises separate from attacks on inference, and then identify which contested premise carries the disagreement
questions.distractor: Invoke the fallacy names available for the opponent’s move, since a defect in the argument defeats the position
questions.correction: Naming fallacies is not an argument, and a defective argument leaves the conclusion standing. The productive move is to isolate the premise or inference on which the disagreement really turns.
